title: Common Apex patterns, anti-patterns, maintainability, and performance
objectives: Name official trigger/service patterns: one trigger per object, bulkification, SOQL/DML outside loops.
Call out anti-patterns: SOQL/DML in loops, recursion without a guard, god classes, hardcoded secrets.
Connect maintainability (thin trigger, testable service) to performance (maps, fewer queries, async choice).
Cite governors (100 SOQL, 150 DML, 10 sendEmail, 50 enqueue) as the performance budget, not invented numbers.
diagnostic_question: A 900-line trigger queries Contacts inside for(Trigger.new), updates each, calls sendEmail per row, and recurses on the same update. Which patterns, anti-patterns, maintainability, and performance changes do you make first?
definition: Common Apex patterns are the official bulk shapes: one trigger per object, collections and maps, SOQL/DML outside loops, thin triggers that call services, and async when the parent transaction cannot finish the work. Anti-patterns invert those. Maintainability is whether a teammate can test and change the service. Performance is staying inside Execution Governors and Limits while remaining correct. ([Triggers and Bulk Best Practices](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bestpract.htm); [Execution Governors and Limits](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm); [Apex Developer Guide](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_dev_guide.htm))
why_it_matters: Most production Apex incidents are anti-patterns that only appear at 200 records. Interviewers want maps, one trigger, a service, tests, and cited governors—not a framework brand name.
sixty_second_explanation: Surgical checklist: one incision plan per object (one trigger), count instruments on a tray (maps, one SOQL, one DML), no fishing expeditions inside the wound (SOQL in a loop), a named procedure card (service class), and a timeout on the clock (governors: 100 SOQL, 150 DML, 10 sendEmail, 50 enqueue). Cowboy surgery is a 900-line trigger that emails and callouts per row and recurses. Maintainability is whether another surgeon can rehearse it in the crash-test lab (APEX-016). Performance is finishing before the 10,000 ms CPU / 10-minute transaction clocks.
deeper_explanation: Triggers and Bulk Best Practices: write triggers to handle 200 records; put SOQL and DML outside loops; use maps keyed by Id; one trigger per object that delegates. Recursion needs a static guard or a field that stops re-entry. ([Trigger best practices](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_bestpract.htm))

Maintainability: thin trigger → handler/service → selector. Services are inherited sharing (APEX-015) and unit-tested (APEX-016). God classes and copy-paste helpers rot. Hardcoded secrets belong in named credentials (APEX-013).

Performance: fewer SOQL/DML, selective filters, maps instead of nested loops, async (APEX-011) when the parent save cannot finish, no callout-after-DML (APEX-013), no FOR UPDATE across callouts (APEX-010). Cite 100 SOQL, 150 DML, 10,000 ms CPU sync, 6 MB heap, 10 sendEmail, 50 enqueueJob from the governors page.

Anti-patterns: SOQL/DML in loops; per-row sendEmail or enqueueJob; SeeAllData tests; without sharing on UI classes; Publish Immediately for inventory; System.debug in loops; empty catch; recursion without a guard.
Frameworks (fflib, trigger frameworks) are optional. Interviews reward the official bulk rules first. Do not invent a Salesforce-required framework name.

mental_model.analogy: A surgical checklist: one incision plan per organ (one trigger), instruments on a tray (maps and bulk DML), no fishing in the wound (SOQL in a loop), a named procedure card (service), and a wall clock (governors). Cowboy surgery is the 900-line trigger.
useful_mapping: one incision plan → one trigger per object
instrument tray → Map<Id, sObject> and list DML
fishing in the wound → SOQL/DML inside for(Trigger.new)
wall clock → 100 SOQL / 150 DML / 10,000 ms CPU
second operating room → Queueable/Batch after commit
where_it_breaks: A framework name is not on the official checklist.
Batch chunk commits are a consistency trade-off, not a performance free lunch.
The surgery analogy does not encode sharing keywords.

teach_back_prompt: Refactor a 900-line trigger aloud into one trigger, a service, maps, one DML, tests, and an async callout—naming the anti-patterns you removed.

claims.claim: Official bulk practice: triggers must handle batches; SOQL and DML belong outside loops; use collections/maps. One trigger per object that delegates is the maintainable shape.
Performance budgets come from Execution Governors and Limits: 100 SOQL, 150 DML, 10,000 ms CPU (sync), 6 MB heap, 10 sendEmail, 50 enqueueJob, 100 callouts.
Maintainability requires tests that assert behavior (Apex Testing), not coverage theater.
Async, security, callouts, and transactions are complementary patterns: do not hide them inside a god trigger.

changed_in_release: Governor numbers above are Summer '26 / API 67.0. Reverify before quoting in a later release. Trigger best-practices page wording should be re-read if a framework debate starts.
unresolved_uncertainty: Salesforce does not require a named trigger framework; do not invent an official fflib mandate.
Exact recursion-guard recipe (static vs custom setting) is design, not a single Guide number.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: One trigger per object, maps, SOQL/DML outside loops, thin service, tests with assertions. Anti-patterns: loops, per-row email/enqueue, recursion, god classes. Performance is the governors table: 100 SOQL, 150 DML, 10 sendEmail, 50 enqueue.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I refactor the 900-line trigger into a handler that calls LAB_OrderService. I collect Ids, one query, map, one DML. Email becomes one sendEmail. Callouts become one Queueable. I add a recursion guard. I write isolated tests for 200 rows. I cite Triggers and Bulk Best Practices and Execution Governors and Limits. I do not sell a framework as official.

terminology.example: Map<Id, Account> from one query, then one update.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Batch Apex: a job type, not the only bulk tool.
terminology.boundary: 200 is the trigger batch size commonly discussed; still cite governors, not unofficial 201.

terminology.precise: One trigger, service layer, map lookup, list DML, Queueable after commit, user mode, isolated tests.
terminology.non_example: Copy-paste the same SOQL into three triggers.
terminology.boundary: Frameworks are optional packaging of these shapes.

terminology.plain: A shape that fails bulk, security, or change.
terminology.precise: SOQL/DML in loops; per-row sendEmail/enqueue; SeeAllData; without sharing on UI; empty catch; recursion; secrets in code.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: LimitException: the usual symptom, not the root.
terminology.boundary: Name the anti-pattern in code review.

terminology.plain: A teammate can change and test it safely.
terminology.precise: Thin trigger, small services, names, isolation tests, no god class.

terminology.plain: Finishing inside official governors with acceptable user time.
terminology.precise: Fewer queries, selective SOQL, maps not nested loops, async offload, no debug floods.
terminology.example: One SOQL for 200 rows vs 200 SOQL.
terminology.non_example: Micro-optimizing a string while leaving SOQL in a loop.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Daily async: org performance, not one trigger.

terminology.plain: Stop the trigger from re-entering forever.
terminology.precise: Static Boolean/set of Ids, or a field that the second pass ignores. Needed when you update the same object.

terminology.plain: Where the work lives instead of the trigger body.
terminology.precise: A class methods can call from trigger, REST, and tests.
terminology.non_example: Business rules pasted into the trigger and a Flow.

terminology.plain: One type that does DML, HTTP, email, and sharing bypass.
terminology.precise: Unmaintainable and untestable. Split by reason to change.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Batch class: allowed to be a job, still should call services.
terminology.boundary: If you cannot write a 200-row test, it is too big.

when_to_use: When a trigger must handle 200 rows: apply official bulkification patterns (maps, SOQL/DML outside loops).
When a class is a god trigger: split a service for maintainability and test it (APEX-016).
When you see per-row sendEmail or enqueueJob: those are anti-patterns against 10 sendEmail and 50 enqueue.
When the same update re-enters the trigger: add a recursion guard, do not empty-catch.
When performance is 'slow': measure LIMIT_USAGE against Execution Governors and Limits, not vibes.
When choosing async: Queueable/Batch from APEX-011, not a new anti-pattern of 200 futures.
when_not_to_use: Do not adopt a trigger framework brand as if the Guide required it.
Do not micro-optimize strings while leaving SOQL in a loop.
Do not treat 75% coverage as maintainability.
Do not 'fix performance' with without sharing on a UI class (APEX-015).
Do not invent governor numbers; quote the official table.
Do not add a second trigger on the same object to avoid touching the first.
configuration_or_code_location: Maps and list DML in the service.
Tests with 200 LAB_ rows inside startTest (APEX-016).

flashcards.back: One trigger per object that delegates to a service.
Collect Ids, one query, Map, no query in the loop.
Static flag/Id set or stop-field; not an empty catch.
100 SOQL, 150 DML, 10 sendEmail, 50 enqueue (plus CPU 10,000 ms sync).
A teammate can write a 200-row isolated test with assertions.
Maps are the official bulk lookup shape.
None required. Bulk rules are official.
One type that does DML, HTTP, email, and sharing bypass—split it.

interview_questions.question: What Apex patterns do you insist on in review?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: One trigger per object, maps, SOQL/DML outside loops, thin service, recursion guard, isolated tests. I cite Triggers and Bulk Best Practices and the governors table.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I walk a 200-row story. I refuse per-row email and enqueue. I do not require fflib by name. I connect security and callout sequencing as part of the pattern set, not extras.
follow_ups: When is a second trigger OK?
weak_answer_warnings: Framework brand as the only answer

interview_questions.question: Name four anti-patterns and the official limit they hit.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: SOQL in a loop (100). DML in a loop (150 statements / row caps). Per-row sendEmail (10). Per-row enqueueJob (50). Bonus: future from batch (0).
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I cite Execution Governors and Limits URLs. I do not invent 10 callouts. I mention CPU 10,000 ms when recursion spins. I offer the map/list fix for each.
interview_questions.example: for (Order o : Trigger.new) { [SELECT ...]; update o; Messaging.sendEmail(...); System.enqueueJob(...); }

interview_questions.question: UI works, Data Loader of 200 fails. Walk it.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I assume a loop anti-pattern. I read the exception trace (APEX-017) to the LAB_ line, then refactor to maps and one DML, then a 200-row test.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I do not blame Data Loader. I check email/enqueue counts. I add Limits assertions. I look for recursion if CPU died. I expire any panic FINEST flag.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Order trigger queries Account per row; 200 rows → 200+ SOQL.

interview_questions.question: How do you keep a trigger maintainable as rules grow?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Thin trigger, service methods named after outcomes, one reason to change per class, tests per behavior, no second stealth trigger.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I split email and HTTP out of the service into collaborators if they grow. I use inherited sharing. I refuse a 900-line method. I do not add a framework unless the team already has one.
tradeoffs: Split too early vs god class
weak_answer_warnings: Another trigger file to avoid merge conflicts only

interview_questions.question: When is Batch a performance pattern vs an anti-pattern escape?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Batch is for QueryLocator volume the parent transaction cannot hold (APEX-011). It is an anti-pattern if you use it to hide a loop you could map in the trigger, because each execute commits separately (APEX-010).
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I ask whether 200 rows in the trigger already fit governors after bulkification. If yes, stay sync. If millions, Batch. I cite 5 active + 100 Holding so I do not spawn Batch from a trigger per row.
interview_questions.example: Nightly archive of millions: Batch. Stamp account name on 200 orders: trigger maps.

interview_questions.question: CPU 10,000 ms on a 50-row update. What anti-pattern?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Recursion or nested loops over queries, not 'need Batch.' I look for trigger-on-update-of-self without a guard, or debug/serialize in a loop.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I use a debug log LIMIT_USAGE and the stack (APEX-017). I add a guard and maps. I write a test that updates once and asserts the service ran once. I cite 10,000 ms sync from the governors page.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Order after-update updates the same order, re-enters until CPU dies.

interview_questions.question: How do patterns compose with security, async, and tests?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Service uses inherited sharing and user mode (APEX-015). Heavy HTTP is Queueable (APEX-011/013). Tests insert LAB_ data, start/stop, mock, assert Limits and fields (APEX-016). Diagnosis uses small logs (APEX-017).
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I refuse a review that only argues framework names. I draw the checklist: bulk, security, async host, test, log. I cite official URLs for any number I speak.
interview_questions.example: LAB_OrderService USER_MODE query, one DML, one Queueable, 200-row test with mock.

interview_questions.question: What will you not claim is an official Salesforce pattern?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: That fflib or a specific trigger framework is required. That 10 callouts is the cap. That SeeAllData is best practice. That without sharing is a performance feature.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I will say the Guide requires bulk-safe triggers, tests, and governors. Everything else is team convention. I mark unofficial lists Needs verification. I keep analogies concrete—surgical checklist, not generic filler.
interview_questions.example: A review comment 'must use fflib or it is not enterprise'—you ask for the official bulk defects instead.
follow_ups: When would you adopt a framework anyway?
How do you document team conventions?
